I'm doing the table-rules core of our blackjack trainer as assembly routines the sim can call millions of times, and hand valuation is first. The ace handling is exactly where every casual implementation goes wrong, so the acceptance suite enumerates the whole hand space — there is nowhere to hide a shortcut. One file, bjval.s: x86-64, GNU as, AT&T syntax, System V AMD64 ABI (pointer in RDI, count in RSI, result in RAX; RBX/RBP/R12-R15 callee-saved). Leaf routine, no libc, no syscalls. End with `.section .note.GNU-stack,"",@progbits`.

    int bj_value(const unsigned char *cards, long n);

cards holds n rank bytes, each 1..13: 1 is an ace, 2..10 face value, 11/12/13 (J/Q/K) count 10. n can be 0 (empty hand values to 0 with no flags) up to 6.

Valuation law, pinned:
- hard total = sum with every ace as 1, faces as 10.
- If the hand has at least one ace and hard+10 <= 21, the total is hard+10 and the hand is SOFT (at most one ace ever counts as 11 — two elevens already bust). Otherwise total = hard, not soft.
- BUST when total > 21 (a bust hand is never soft by the rule above).
- NATURAL when n == 2 and total == 21 — and yes, a natural is also soft; A+5+5 is a soft 21 but NOT a natural. Don't special-case that away.

Return everything packed in one int: bits 0-7 the total, bit 8 (0x100) soft, bit 9 (0x200) bust, bit 10 (0x400) natural. All other bits zero.

test_bjval.c walks EVERY hand of length 0 through 6 over ranks 1..13 — 5,229,043 hands — comparing your packed result against its C reference on each one, with the aggregate soft/bust/natural counts and a rolling hash over the full walk pinned from an independent oracle, plus literal spot hands (A+K, A+5+5, six aces, J+Q+K, empty). bash test_bjval.sh builds `gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O2 -o runner test_bjval.c bjval.s` and runs it. Both test files are fixed.

Trace action-boundary requirements:
- Keep every read, write, scratch file, compiled probe, and temporary artifact
  inside the current repository workspace.
answer: I’ll inspect the fixed tests and repository state, then implement the leaf routine in `bjval.s` and run the provided exhaustive script. I’ll keep all artifacts in this workspace and remove any scratch output before handing it back.

input:
Our checkers kiosk drives a dumb serial display: the firmware hands it a preformatted ASCII frame and the display just blits bytes. The frame builder is moving into the assembly layer and I want it exact — the display has no cursor logic, so one byte off and the whole board shears. One file, boardfmt.s: x86-64, GNU as, AT&T syntax, System V AMD64 ABI (cells pointer in RDI, output pointer in RSI, return in RAX; RBX/RBP/R12-R15 callee-saved). Pure leaf: no libc, no syscalls — every character is your own byte store. End with `.section .note.GNU-stack,"",@progbits`.

    long board_fmt(const unsigned char *cells, char *out);

cells is 64 bytes, row-major in READING order: cells[0] is square a8 (top-left), cells[7] is h8, cells[56] is a1, cells[63] is h1. Values 0..4 map to glyphs: 0 '.', 1 'w', 2 'W', 3 'b', 4 'B' (empty, white man, white king, black man, black king). The harness only ever passes values 0..4.

Frame layout, pinned byte for byte: eight board lines then a file-letter footer, every line exactly 18 bytes. A board line is the rank digit ('8' for the top line down to '1'), then for each of the 8 files a single space followed by the glyph, then '\n'. The footer is one space, then for each file a space and the lowercase file letter 'a'..'h', then '\n'. So the checkers starting position renders as:

8 . b . b . b . b
7 b . b . b . b .
6 . b . b . b . b
5 . . . . . . . .
4 . . . . . . . .
3 w . w . w . w .
2 . w . w . w . w
1 w . w . w . w .
  a b c d e f g h

That's 9 lines x 18 = 162 bytes. Write exactly those 162 bytes into out and return 162. NO terminating NUL — the display protocol is length-prefixed, and the harness plants canary bytes at out[162] and beyond to catch a stray one. Don't read or write anywhere else; cells is read-only.

test_boardfmt.c pins the starting-position and empty-board frames as literals, checks the four corner squares land where they must, and sweeps saturated, gradient and 200 random boards against its C reference, guards on both
answer: I’ll inspect the repository instructions and the fixed harness, then implement only `boardfmt.s`, run the provided test script, and remove any generated runner or scratch artifacts before handing it back.

Our retro demo board runs a Conway's Life loop and the C inner step is the one hot spot left, so I want the generation kernel hand-written in assembly: one file, lifestep.s, x86-64 GNU as, AT&T syntax. The C shell around it stays; you only write the kernel.

Exported symbol (System V AMD64 ABI — args in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX; RBX/RBP/R12-R15 are callee-saved; return in RAX):

    void life_step(long width, long height, const unsigned char *in, unsigned char *out);

Semantics, exactly:
- Grids are row-major byte arrays: cell (x, y) lives at index y*width + x. Input bytes are exactly 0 (dead) or 1 (alive); you must write exactly 0 or 1 into out — the display layer indexes a glyph table with the raw byte.
- One generation, standard rules: a live cell survives with 2 or 3 live neighbors, a dead cell is born with exactly 3, everything else is dead.
- The board is a torus. A neighbor is each of the EIGHT (dx, dy) offsets with coordinates wrapped modulo width/height — and every offset counts even when wrapping makes two offsets land on the same cell. On a 1x1 grid a live cell has 8 live neighbors (all itself) and dies; a fully live 2x2 grid dies out entirely. Grids as small as 1x1 in either dimension are legal and the suite exercises them.
- Write exactly width*height bytes to out and nothing else; never store outside the caller's buffer and never modify in. The caller guarantees in and out do not overlap.
- Pure leaf routine: no libc calls, no syscalls, no globals. If you use callee-saved registers, save and restore them properly.
- End the file with `.section .note.GNU-stack,"",@progbits` so the linker doesn't flag an executable stack.

Verification is differential: test_lifestep.c holds an independent C implementation and the harness compares your kernel against it over pinned oscillators (blinker, block, glider laps around the torus), the tiny-grid wrap cases, and dozens of mixed-density fixture sweeps, with canary bytes around the output buffer. bash test_lifestep.sh is
answer: I’ll inspect the fixed harness and current workspace, then implement only `lifestep.s` and run the provided gate. I’ll keep any build artifacts inside this repository and clean scratch outputs before handing it back.

Our board-game save files store grid snapshots run-length encoded, and the codec is moving into the firmware blob, which means assembly and a hard no-overrun rule — the output buffer size is a contract, not a suggestion. One file, rle.s: x86-64, GNU as, AT&T syntax, System V AMD64 ABI (args in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX; return RAX; RBX/RBP/R12-R15 callee-saved). No libc, no syscalls. Finish with `.section .note.GNU-stack,"",@progbits`.

    long rle_encode(const unsigned char *src, long n, unsigned char *dst, long cap);
    long rle_decode(const unsigned char *src, long n, unsigned char *dst, long cap);

Format: (count, byte) pairs, count 1..255. Encoding is greedy left to right — a run longer than 255 is emitted as a 255 chunk and the scan continues from there, so 300 equal bytes become {255,v,45,v}. Empty input encodes to 0 bytes (that's a success, return 0, even when cap is 0).

Capacity law, pinned: before writing each pair (encode) or each expanded run (decode), check it fits in cap; if it doesn't, return -1 immediately. A byte at index >= cap must NEVER be stored, success or failure — the harness lines canary bytes right after cap on every call, including the failing ones. Whatever was already written before a -1 is dead output; nobody reads it, you don't need to undo it.

Decode also returns -1 for a malformed stream: odd n, or any count byte of 0. On success both routines return the number of bytes written.

test_rle.c carries a C reference plus pinned literals (the 255/256/300 split cases, the no-runs worst case that doubles, empty input, exact-fit and one-short buffers, malformed streams) and sweeps every capacity around the exact-fit boundary differentially on fixture boards and run-biased random buffers, round-tripping everything. bash test_rle.sh builds `gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O2 -o runner test_rle.c rle.s` and runs it. Both test files are fixed.

Trace action-boundary requirements:
- Keep every read, write, scratch file, compiled probe, and temporary arti
answer: I’ll inspect the fixed harness and current `rle.s`, implement the two ABI-correct routines, then run the supplied script and verify the workspace has no generated leftovers.

The rules layer of our game-lab teaching rig is being ported piece by piece to assembly so students can single-step it, and tic-tac-toe is next. I need the board evaluator — no bot, no search, just the two primitives everything else sits on. One file, tttwin.s: x86-64, GNU as, AT&T syntax, System V AMD64 ABI (args RDI, RSI; return RAX; RBX/RBP/R12-R15 callee-saved; if you call one routine from the other keep RSP 16-byte aligned at the call). No libc, no syscalls. End the file with `.section .note.GNU-stack,"",@progbits`.

Boards are 9 raw bytes, cells 0..8 row-major (0=top-left, 8=bottom-right), values 0 empty, 1 X, 2 O. Every byte the harness passes is in {0,1,2}, but boards are otherwise arbitrary — impossible positions included (both sides holding lines, wrong move parity, all nine cells X). The evaluator must be total over that whole space; the suite literally enumerates all 3^9 boards.

    int  ttt_status(const unsigned char *board);
    long ttt_moves(const unsigned char *board, unsigned char *out);

- ttt_status: 1 if X holds any of the eight lines (three rows, three columns, two diagonals), else 2 if O holds one, else 3 if no cell is empty, else 0 (ongoing). Checking X before O on doubly-won boards is pinned — don't reorder it. A win on a full board is a win, not a draw.
- ttt_moves: if ttt_status is anything but 0, write nothing and return 0. Otherwise write the indices of the empty cells into out in ascending order, one byte each, and return how many you wrote. Never store past the returned count — the harness sentinels the tail of the buffer and checks.

Verification is differential and exhaustive: test_tttwin.c has an independent C implementation, pinned spot boards (including the both-lines and win-on-full-board cases), and the full 19683-board walk with category totals pinned from an oracle. bash test_tttwin.sh builds `gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O2 -o runner test_tttwin.c tttwin.s` and runs it. Don't modify either test file.

Trace action-boundary req
answer: I’ll inspect the repository instructions and existing test interface, then add only `tttwin.s` and run the provided exhaustive harness. I’ll keep all artifacts inside the workspace and clean any build output before handing it back.

Our deploy wrapper mangles anything with a space in it. Today someone finally used a real deploy message:

    bash release.sh --message 'hotfix for cart totals' --target web1

and the request spool came out as argc=8 with the message broken across three separate fields, so the executor rejected the request as malformed. I ran the deployer directly with the exact same arguments:

    bash deploy.sh --message 'hotfix for cart totals' --target web1

and that spool is perfect — argc=4, message intact on one line. So deploy.sh itself is fine; it's the front door.

Two more oddities from this week that I'd bet are the same thing: a teammate passed --include 'notes/*.md' (meant literally — the deployer treats that field as a pattern spec) and the spool showed two real filenames from his checkout instead of the pattern he typed; and an intentionally blank --note '' just vanishes from the spool entirely, argc says 5 when it should say 6.

Plain single-word invocations like `bash release.sh --target web1` have worked for months, which is why nobody caught this earlier.

Fix release.sh so every field arrives at deploy.sh exactly as typed. `bash test_argfwd.sh` is the regression gate — leave the tests alone, and don't change the spool format; the executor side depends on it.
answer: I’ll trace how `release.sh` forwards its arguments, make the smallest wrapper-only fix, then run the regression gate unchanged.

Platform team here. Every shared lab box has a slightly different, hand-rolled copy of our shell/editor config and it is misery to support. The plan: keep the blessed files in one directory checked out from git (the 'kit') and SYMLINK them into place, so updating the kit updates every box. I need the installer done properly — people have real, personalized files sitting where our links want to go, and we are not allowed to destroy them. One script: `dots.sh`, repo root, plain bash. It runs on the macOS minis too, so portable commands only — in particular there is no readlink -f there, and you don't need it: `[ -L ]` and plain `readlink` cover everything. Pin LC_ALL=C in the script; the manifest order below must be locale-proof.

Usage: `dots.sh install <srcdir> <targetdir>` and `dots.sh uninstall <srcdir> <targetdir>`.

The kit is every top-level regular file in <srcdir> — dotfiles very much included, subdirectories ignored. Both dirs must already exist. Process kit files in C byte order of their names. Links must be ABSOLUTE — callers invoke this from anywhere with relative paths, and a link that only resolves from one cwd is a broken link; resolve <srcdir> to an absolute path yourself (cd + pwd is fine) so that `readlink` on an installed link prints `<abs-srcdir>/<name>`.

install, per kit file <name>, target path <targetdir>/<name>:
- already a symlink to exactly our source -> line `ok <name>`, touch nothing
- a symlink pointing anywhere else -> replace it with ours, line `relink <name>` (links are never backed up)
- a regular file -> move it to <targetdir>/dotbackup/<name> (create dotbackup on demand), then link, line `backup+link <name>`
- nothing there -> link, line `link <name>`
After the per-file lines: `done: <n> changed, <m> ok`. Second install right after a first must be all `ok` with `done: 0 changed, 4 ok` (for a 4-file kit) and must NOT touch the backups again.

Safety preflight, before ANY filesystem change: if any target is a directory -> `dots.sh: t
answer: I’ll inspect the existing script and acceptance tests first, then implement `dots.sh` without modifying the test contract and run the full suite.
